passages.happening:
Luke opens with one long, careful sentence. Many people, he says, have already tried to write down the story of “the things that have been fulfilled among us” (verse 1). These things were handed down by people who saw them from the start, “the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word” (verse 2).

Luke has checked everything from the beginning. Now he will write it out in order for a man called Theophilus, “so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
No other Gospel starts like this. Matthew begins with a family tree, Mark with a voice in the desert, John with the beginning of the world. Luke begins the way an educated Greek writer might begin a serious book: by saying how it was made.

A first reader would notice three things. Luke is not an eyewitness himself, and he says so; he is a careful collector of what eyewitnesses said. He has done research. And he writes to a real reader with a real need. Theophilus has been taught about Jesus already. Luke wants that teaching to rest on solid ground.

‘Most excellent’ was a title for people of rank; in Acts it is used for Roman governors (Acts 24:3, 26:25). Who Theophilus was, and why Luke wrote to him, is explained on the book page.
passages.ot: ‘Fulfilled’ is the key word. Luke is not just telling stories about a good man. He is saying that what God promised in Scripture, through Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms, has now come true. The book ends on the same note, with the risen Jesus saying that “everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (24:44). The first sentence and the last chapter hold the book between them.
passages.hard: If Luke used earlier writings, does that make his book less inspired? Christians have not thought so. Luke is open about his method: he gathered, checked and arranged. The Bible never says its writers took dictation. It shows God working through real people doing real work, including research. For many readers, Luke's honesty about his sources is a reason to trust him more, not less.
passages.asks: Luke wrote so that a believer could be sure. Faith is not the same as guessing, and it does not grow by refusing to ask questions. What questions do you carry about the things you have been taught? Luke invites you to bring them, and to look at the evidence with him.

passages.t: A priest, a prayer, and an angel at the altar
passages.happening:
The story begins ‘in the time of Herod king of Judea’ (verse 5). Zechariah is a priest, and his wife Elizabeth comes from the priestly family of Aaron too. Both are “righteous in the sight of God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and decrees of the Lord” (verse 6). But they have no children, and now they are old.

Zechariah's group of priests is on duty at the temple in Jerusalem. He is chosen by lot to go into the holy place and burn incense, while a crowd prays outside. Suddenly an angel stands beside the altar. Zechariah is terrified.

The angel says, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard” (verse 13). Elizabeth will have a son. He is to be called John. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit from before his birth, and he will turn many in Israel back to God, going ahead of the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The priests of Israel were many, so they took turns. The Bible lists twenty-four groups, and the group of Abijah, Zechariah's group, was the eighth (1 Chronicles 24:10). Each group served at the temple for a set time and then went home.

Burning the incense in the holy place was a great honour. The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, says the priests cast lots for it among those who had never done it before (Mishnah Tamid 5:2). So for many priests it came once in a lifetime, if it came at all. This may have been the greatest day of Zechariah's working life.

Being childless was a deep grief then, and a public shame. People had no pensions; children cared for you in old age and carried on your name. And many people assumed that if a couple had no children, God must be displeased with them. Elizabeth later speaks of ‘my disgrace among the people’ (verse 25).

Luke will not let that idea stand. Before he says they had no children, he says they were righteous and blameless. Their childlessness was not a punishment. It was a sorrow that faithful people carried for years.
passages.ot:
Luke's first hearers would have known this kind of story by heart. An old couple with no child; a promise; a son born against all hope. It is the story of Abraham and Sarah, who were also “well along in years” (Genesis 18:11). It is the story of Hannah, who prayed in the house of God for a son and gave him back to the LORD (1 Samuel 1:11).

The angel's words about John point to the last page of the Old Testament. Malachi promised that God would send “Elijah the prophet” before the Day of the LORD, and that “he will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children” (Malachi 4:5-6). The angel quotes that line about John (verse 17). After centuries of waiting, the promise is starting to come true.

John is not to drink wine or strong drink (verse 15). That echoes the vow of a Nazirite, a person set apart for God (Numbers 6:3), and the promise to Samson's mother (Judges 13:4-5).
passages.hard:
Why did God wait so long to answer? Luke does not say. He says only that the prayer ‘has been heard’. It may be a prayer Zechariah had long since stopped praying.

A word of care. This story ends in joy for one couple. It does not promise a child to every couple who prays for one. Many faithful people long for children and never have them, or lose them before birth. If that is your grief, notice what Luke says first: Zechariah and Elizabeth were righteous in God's sight before any child came. Childlessness is not a judgment from God, and it does not measure your faith. Your longing is seen. If the grief is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor.
passages.asks: Zechariah was doing his ordinary duty when God broke in. He had nearly stopped hoping. Is there an old prayer you have quietly given up on? This passage does not promise you a particular answer. It does promise that God hears, and that long waiting is not the same as being forgotten.

passages.t: ‘How can I be sure?’ Silence, then Elizabeth's joy
passages.happening:
Zechariah cannot take it in. “How can I be sure of this?” he asks. “I am an old man, and my wife is well along in years” (verse 18).

The angel gives his name: ‘I am Gabriel.’ He says, “I stand in the presence of God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to bring you this good news” (verse 19). Because Zechariah did not believe, he will be unable to speak until the promise comes true.

Outside, the people wonder why he is taking so long. When he comes out he cannot speak. He can only make signs, and they realize he has seen a vision. When his time of duty ends, he goes home. Elizabeth becomes pregnant and stays out of sight for five months. She says, “The Lord has done this for me. In these days He has shown me favor and taken away my disgrace among the people” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The crowd outside was waiting for the priest to come out. Zechariah had gone in to burn incense while the people prayed, and now he cannot even speak to them. The great day of his life ends in silence.

Gabriel was a name the hearers knew. He is one of only two angels named in the Hebrew Bible, both in the book of Daniel. There, Gabriel came to Daniel ‘about the time of the evening sacrifice’ (Daniel 9:21), the hour of prayer. Here he comes at the hour of incense.

Elizabeth's words would have moved anyone who knew what childlessness cost a woman then. Her shame had been public. Neighbours had seen, and some had talked. Now God has removed it.
passages.ot: Elizabeth's words echo Rachel, Jacob's wife, who had no children for years. When at last she bore a son, she said, “God has taken away my shame” (Genesis 30:23). Hearers would also remember Sarah, who laughed at the promise of a son in her old age, and was asked, “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). Zechariah's question is Sarah's laugh in another form.
passages.hard: Why is Zechariah punished for asking a question, when Mary also asks one a few verses later (verse 34) and is not? Readers have long noticed this. The answer most give is that the two questions are different. Zechariah asks for proof: how can I be sure? Mary believes and asks how it will happen. Luke does not make Zechariah a villain; he has just called him righteous. His doubt is the doubt of a faithful man worn down by years of waiting. Even his silence is a kind of sign, and it ends in praise (verse 64).
passages.asks: Zechariah's doubt did not stop God's promise. It only stopped his mouth for a while. If you find it hard to believe now, perhaps harder than you once did, take heart. God is not undone by our doubts. But notice the difference between asking God to prove himself and asking him to show you the way. Which is your question?

passages.happening:
Six months later, God sends Gabriel to Nazareth, a town in Galilee. He comes to a young woman named Mary, who is pledged to marry Joseph, a man of David's family. “Greetings, you who are highly favored,” the angel says. “The Lord is with you” (verse 28).

Mary is deeply troubled. The angel tells her not to be afraid. She will have a son and name him Jesus. “He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David” (verse 32), and his kingdom will never end.

Mary asks, “How can this be,” and then, “since I am a virgin?” (verse 34). The angel answers, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God” (verse 35). Elizabeth, too old for children, is already six months pregnant. “For no word from God will ever fail” (verse 37).

Mary answers, “I am the Lord's servant.” And then, “May it happen to me according to your word” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The contrast is sharp. The first angel came to an old priest in the holiest room of the grandest building in the land. The second comes to a young woman in a small village. Nazareth was a farming village of perhaps a few hundred people, never mentioned in the Old Testament.

Mary is ‘pledged in marriage’. A Jewish marriage then came in two steps. First came betrothal, a binding promise; from then on the couple counted as husband and wife, though they did not yet live together. Later came the wedding, when the bride moved to her husband's home. The titles Gabriel uses, ‘Son of the Most High’ and ‘Son of God’, were not new to Jewish ears. A damaged scroll found near the Dead Sea, known as 4Q246, speaks of a coming figure who will be called ‘son of God’ and ‘son of the Most High’. Scholars argue over whether it means a coming king or an enemy who claims those titles. Either way, the words were in the air. Gabriel ties them to David's throne: this child is the promised king.
passages.ot:
The promise of David's throne goes back to 2 Samuel 7, where God promised David, “Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever” (2 Samuel 7:16). By Jesus' day there had been no son of David on a throne for about six hundred years. Gabriel says the promise is about to be kept.

‘The power of the Most High will overshadow you’ may recall the cloud that covered the tabernacle when God's glory filled it (Exodus 40:34-35). God's own presence comes to rest, this time in a young woman.

And the angel's last words, ‘no word from God will ever fail’, answer the old question put to Sarah: “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14).
passages.hard:
Two questions are worth facing.

The first is the virgin conception. Luke says plainly that Mary had not slept with any man, and that the child was conceived by the Holy Spirit. Matthew tells the same from Joseph's side (Matthew 1:18-25); the two accounts are independent. Skeptics answer that miracles cannot be shown by history and that the ancient world told of great men with divine fathers. Christians answer that those stories tell of gods fathering children with women, and Luke tells nothing like that, and that if God made the world, a new beginning in a womb is not beyond him. The Apostles' Creed confesses that Jesus was ‘conceived by the Holy Ghost, born of the Virgin Mary’. The site confesses it with them.

The second is the greeting. The Greek word in verse 28 means one who has been shown grace or favour by God. Jerome's Latin Bible rendered it ‘full of grace’, and the Hail Mary prays in those words. Catholic teaching reads it as a sign that God filled Mary with grace from the start of her life, which is part of its teaching on the Immaculate Conception, that Mary was kept free from original sin. Most Protestants translate it ‘highly favored’ or ‘favored one’ and read it as God's free kindness to her, not as a claim about her sinlessness. Both sides agree on the heart of the verse: Mary is chosen by grace, and ‘the Lord is with you’.
passages.asks: Mary's question was honest, and her answer was brave. She knew what a pregnancy before the wedding might cost her: her name, her marriage, perhaps her safety. She said yes anyway. What would it mean for you to say, about something God is asking that you do not fully understand, ‘I am the Lord's servant’?

passages.happening:
Mary hurries south to the hill country of Judea, to the home of Zechariah and Elizabeth. When Elizabeth hears Mary's greeting, the baby jumps in her womb, and Elizabeth is filled with the Holy Spirit.

She cries out, “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb” (verse 42). Then she asks, “Why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (verse 43). And she blesses Mary for her faith: “Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord's word to her will be fulfilled” (verse 45).
passages.hearers:
The trip from Nazareth to the hill country around Jerusalem was a long one, several days on foot. Mary does not wait. Perhaps she went to see the sign Gabriel had given her. Perhaps she needed the one person who would believe her.

Picture the meeting. An old woman, pregnant against all hope. A young woman, pregnant without a man. Two women carrying news no one else would believe. And it is the older woman, from a priest's house, who honours the younger.

Elizabeth calls Mary ‘the mother of my Lord’. For a Jewish woman, ‘Lord’ was the word used in the Greek Bible for God himself. Elizabeth sees, before anyone else, who Mary's child is.
passages.ot:
Elizabeth's blessing echoes an old song of Israel. In the book of Judges, Deborah sings, “Most blessed among women is Jael” (Judges 5:24). Jael was a woman through whom God rescued his people. Mary will be too, but by giving birth, not by a sword.

Some readers also hear the story of the ark of God, the chest that stood for God's presence. David asked, “How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?” (2 Samuel 6:9), much as Elizabeth asks why the mother of her Lord should come to her. The ark then stayed in a house for three months (2 Samuel 6:11), as Mary stays with Elizabeth for three months (verse 56). If Luke meant the echo, he is saying that God's presence now travels in Mary.
passages.hard: How much honour should Christians give to Mary? Here Elizabeth, filled with the Spirit, calls her blessed, and Mary herself will say that “all generations will call me blessed” (verse 48). Catholic and Orthodox Christians give Mary great honour and ask her prayers, though they distinguish that from the worship due to God alone. Many Protestants honour her as a model of faith and are careful to keep the focus on her Son. All can agree with Elizabeth on the reason she is blessed: she believed God's word.
passages.asks: Elizabeth could have felt overshadowed. Her own miracle was eclipsed by a greater one. Instead she rejoiced. Whose good news could you celebrate today, even if it is bigger than your own? And who in your life needs one person to believe them?

passages.happening:
Mary answers with a song. It is called the Magnificat, from its first word in Latin. “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior” (verses 46-47). God has looked kindly on his humble servant. From now on all generations will call her blessed, because the Mighty One has done great things for her.

Then the song widens from Mary to the world. God's mercy reaches every generation of those who fear him. “He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty” (verses 52-53). He has helped Israel, as he promised Abraham.

Mary stays with Elizabeth about three months, then goes home.
passages.hearers:
Mary sings about God's great reversal: the proud scattered, rulers pulled down, the humble lifted up, the hungry fed, the rich sent away with nothing. She sings it as though it has already happened, in the past tense. In the child she carries, God has begun it, and it is as good as done.

To a poor village girl in an occupied land, these were not gentle words. Herod sat on a throne. Rome ruled the world. Mary sings that God brings rulers down.

Christians have read this song in two wrong ways. Some make it only about the inner life, as though ‘the hungry’ just means the spiritually hungry. But Mary speaks of real thrones, real food and real riches. Others make it a party programme, as if God were on one side of today's arguments. But Mary also speaks of the proud ‘in the thoughts of their hearts’ (verse 51), which can be anyone. The song judges every reader who is comfortable, and comforts every reader who is low.
passages.ot:
Mary's song is woven from the Old Testament, above all from the prayer of Hannah, who had no children until God gave her Samuel. Hannah sang, “My heart rejoices in the LORD” (1 Samuel 2:1). She sang that God “humbles and He exalts” (1 Samuel 2:7), and “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap” (1 Samuel 2:8). Mary takes up Hannah's song a thousand years later.

There are echoes of the Psalms too. ‘Holy is His name’ recalls Psalm 111:9, “holy and awesome is His name.” And God's mercy that “extends to those who fear Him” is a line of Psalm 103:17. And the song ends where Israel's story began, with God's promise to Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3).
passages.hard: Is it right to sing that God sends the rich away empty? Luke does not soften it, and neither should we. Mary is not saying that money damns people and poverty saves them. She is saying that God sees who is crushed and who is doing the crushing, and that he will set things right. Throughout his book Luke shows rich people saved too, when they turn and share (19:8-9). The warning is real, and so is the welcome. Christians in every age and every party have had to hear this song as a word to themselves before they use it against others.
passages.asks: Mary calls herself humble, and sings that God lifts up the humble. Where do you stand in her song? If you are low, she sings that God has not forgotten you. If you are comfortable, she sings a warning. Most of us are both. What would it look like to rejoice in God the way she did, with nothing to offer but trust?

passages.happening:
Elizabeth has her baby, a son. Her neighbours and relatives hear that the Lord has been kind to her, and they share her joy.

On the eighth day they come to circumcise the boy. They expect him to be named Zechariah, after his father. But Elizabeth says, “No! He shall be called John” (verse 60). No one in the family has that name, they object, so they make signs to his father. Zechariah asks for a writing tablet and writes, “His name is John” (verse 63).

At once his mouth is opened and he begins to praise God. Fear and wonder spread through the hill country. Everyone asks, “What then will this child become?” (verse 66).
passages.hearers:
The law of Moses said a boy was to be circumcised on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12). Luke shows the naming done on the same day, as with Jesus in 2:21.

Sons were usually named after a father or a grandfather. Names kept a family's memory alive. So when Elizabeth chooses a name no one in the family has, the relatives push back. This was not only a family argument; it was a break with custom.

Zechariah asks for a writing tablet. His four words settle it. He has obeyed the angel at last, and his silence ends.

‘John’ comes from the Hebrew Yohanan, meaning ‘the LORD has been gracious’. The name itself tells the family's story.
passages.ot:
The relatives' question, ‘What then will this child become?’, sounds like the questions asked about children in the Old Testament who were born by God's special gift. Samuel was born to Hannah and given to the LORD (1 Samuel 1:20-28). Samson's birth was announced by an angel (Judges 13). Each grew up to serve God at a turning point in Israel's history. Hearers would expect the same of John.

Circumcision itself was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:9-12). John enters that covenant on his eighth day. He will spend his life calling Israel back to it.
passages.hard: Why does it matter what the boy is called? Because the name came from God through the angel (verse 13). Zechariah's first act after his silence is to obey. Some readers see his silence as a punishment; others see it also as a mercy, a time for a doubting man to watch God keep his word. Both can be true.
passages.asks: Elizabeth and Zechariah went against family custom because God had spoken. Sometimes faithfulness means disappointing people we love. Is there a place where you need to choose God's word over what everyone expects?

passages.happening:
Zechariah is filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesies. His song is called the Benedictus, from its first word in Latin. “Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, because He has visited and redeemed His people” (verse 68).

He sings of a ‘horn of salvation’ raised up in David's family, of rescue from enemies, and of God remembering his promise to Abraham, so that his people can serve him without fear.

Then he turns to his baby son. “And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High; for you will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him” (verse 76). John will help people know salvation through the forgiveness of their sins, because of God's tender mercy. A new dawn is coming, to shine on those in darkness and guide their feet into peace.

The chapter ends with John growing up and living in the wilderness until he appears in public.
passages.hearers:
A horn, in the Bible, is a picture of strength, like the horns of a bull. A ‘horn of salvation’ is a strong rescuer. Zechariah is a priest, from the family of Aaron. But the rescuer he sings about comes from the house of David, the royal family. He is not singing about his own son first. He is singing about Mary's.

Many Jews in that day longed for rescue from foreign rulers. Zechariah's song speaks of enemies too. But notice where it lands: salvation comes ‘through the forgiveness of their sins’ (verse 77). The deepest enemy is not Rome.

‘The Dawn will visit us from on high’ (verse 78) is a picture of sunrise. In a world without electric light, everyone knew the long dark hours before morning. Zechariah sings that the night is nearly over.

Some have wondered whether John grew up near the community whose scrolls were found by the Dead Sea, since he lived in the wilderness (verse 80). That is only a guess. Luke says simply that he lived in the desert until the time came.
passages.ot: Almost every line of this song comes from the Old Testament. God's ‘holy covenant’ and ‘the oath He swore to our father Abraham’ (verses 72-73) recall the promise of Genesis 22:16-18. The ‘horn’ for David recalls Psalm 132:17, “There I will make a horn grow for David.” John going ‘before the Lord to prepare the way’ points to Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3. And the light for those ‘in darkness and in the shadow of death’ recalls Isaiah 9:2, “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light.”
passages.hard: Zechariah says his son will go before ‘the Lord’. In the Old Testament, the one who comes after the messenger is God himself (Malachi 3:1). In Luke, the one who comes after John is Jesus. Luke is quietly saying something astonishing about who Jesus is. He does not explain it yet. He lets the songs say more than the singers knew.
passages.asks: Zechariah's first words after months of silence are praise. What has God done for you that you have not yet thanked him for? And if you are sitting in a long darkness, his song is for you: the dawn is coming, and it comes from God's tender mercy, not from your strength.
